title: Quantum Advantage for Two-Party Differential Privacy
abstract: We introduce information-theoretically private quantum protocols for two-party Hamming distance when both parties must output the same estimate. Classically, for input length $n$, information-theoretic protocols require $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ error under pure differential privacy and $Ω(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ error under strong approximate differential privacy, whereas computational security permits $O(1)$ error. In Klauck's honest, nonpreemptive, message-preserving model, we give an $O(n)$-communication quantum protocol with pure $\varepsilon$ quantum differential privacy (QDP) and expected error at most $\frac{2}{\sinh \varepsilon}+γ$, for every $γ>0$. For approximate $(\varepsilon, δ)$ QDP, an exact hockey-stick divergence calculation yields strictly smaller error, while preserving the $O(1)$-versus-$Ω(\sqrt{n}/\log n)$ separation for $δ=o(1/n)$. Thus, quantum communication achieves $O(1)$ information-theoretic error, matching the accuracy available classically only under computational assumptions.   The main construction uses a guarded coherent round trip and an equal-Gram rigidity principle that prevents an honest player from retaining input-dependent complementary information. We separate this model from weaker prescribed-channel privacy, which already admits an exact classical realization, and from fully retention-robust security, against which measurement-and-abort attacks remain possible. Therefore, we identify preservation of non-orthogonal quantum messages as a resource for privacy.
summary: This work develops quantum protocols to compute the Hamming distance privately between two parties, achieving an $O(1)$ error rate under information-theoretic privacy guarantees. This significantly surpasses the classical lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ error required by classical protocols. The advantage stems from leveraging quantum mechanics in a specific honest-but-curious communication model.
main_problem: The paper addresses achieving information-theoretically private quantum protocols for computing the two-party Hamming distance when both parties must output the same estimate.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that quantum communication can achieve an $O(1)$ information-theoretic error rate, matching the accuracy available classically only under computational assumptions, by exploiting quantum principles in the Klauck's honest, nonpreemptive model.
method: The construction utilizes a 'guarded coherent round trip' and relies on the 'equal-Gram rigidity principle' to ensure privacy by preventing the observer from retaining input-dependent complementary information.
model_or_system: The analysis is set within quantum communication protocols, comparing different security models: Prescribed-channel (PC), Klauck's honest nonpreemptive view (KHNP), and Retention-robust (RR).
key_observables: Expected error in estimating the Hamming distance, Quantum Differential Privacy (QDP) parameters ($\epsilon, \delta$), and communication complexity ($O(n)$ qubits/bits).
important_parameters: Input length $n$, privacy parameters $\epsilon$ and $\delta$, and the separation between classical $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ and quantum $O(1)$ error bounds.
main_assumptions: The quantum advantage is specific to the KHNP model and relies on the non-copyability of non-orthogonal quantum messages; it is not guaranteed against fully malicious retention-robust attacks.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares classical DP protocols showing the $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ gap; Figure 2 illustrates the quantum advantage in the KHNP model using non-orthogonal messages.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem gap classically, then introduces the quantum protocol using the guarded coherent round trip and rigidity principle. It details results for pure QDP and approximate QDP, concluding with a comparison to the fully retention-robust baseline.
why_interesting: The core concept of using quantum information theory (like non-orthogonality) to break classical information-theoretic lower bounds in privacy-preserving computation is highly relevant to quantum cryptography and secure quantum computation.
